Attribute

slides.title: data actually makes more sense if it is displayed symbolically rather than with their real value (hex, dec, eng units).
slides.body:
o
Network node
consists of one CAN Controller and
a
transceiver in an ECU. An ECU may contain more than one
node. A node may have a ID and it is responsible for a set of
functions of that
ECU.
o
Message
is a container holding a block of data
transmitted into the bus. This block of data is shown
numerically in CANoe in either hex or dec. To display the
message name and its data field, in engineering units or
symbolically, the message has to be defined in the
database.

slides.title: Symbolic access CAPL
slides.body:
o
The database basically follows the architecture
on
the right.
o
Signals
are the actual data objects to be exchanged
between nodes, and are encoded in the data field of
CAN messages. Signals typically occupy most or all of
a CAN message data bytes, and they must not overlap.
In the database, signals can have parameters for
conversion of raw data to physical units (also known as
an engineering unit).
o
Environment variables
are data objects global to
the CANoe environment, and are used to link the
functions of a
CANoe panel to CAPL programs.

slides.title: PANEL CAPL
slides.body:
o
Panels are not used to exchange data between simulated
network nodes. That is, environment
variables are not capable of exchanging data between a simulated node and a real module. The
only way to exchange data in a CAN network is by using a CAN message.

slides.title: o Environment variables are global and may be used in every network node in a CANoe configuration. Use them to exchange

communicate

o
Environment variables have to be assigned a data
type in the database. The choice of
data type includes INTEGER, FLOAT, STRING, and DATA. STRING is used for ASCII.
DATA is used to store values in term of bytes.

slides.title: Functions CAPL
slides.body:
o
CAPL allows you log portions of a simulation. When the conditions to begin logging are met, call
the
startLogging()
function in the CAPL code.
o
By using CAPL to control logging, all the time settings
in the configuration of the Logging block can be
offset by the settings that were set with a CAPL program. The pretrigger time is the period of time during
which bus activity is recorded before logging is triggered. The posttrigger time is the period of time
during which bus activity is recorded after logging is stopped.
o
In the following example, pressing key ‘1’ starts
logging with a 1000 ms pre-trigger time, and key ‘2’
is used to stop logging with a 2000 ms post-trigger time.

system clock initializes. It works independently of the Window timers.

To

This

To calculate the time difference between two messages,

o
If you need to reference the Window clock, the

and

o
For
controlling
processing
time
variation,
provides
two

and

.
The

constant
deviation
between
–100%
and
+100%
for
all
timers
used
in
a
network
node.
The
setJitter()
function,
however,
sets
the
fluctuation
interval
between
–100%
and
+100%.
Setting
either
function
will
reset the other. To set both the drift and the jitter, use the
setJitter()
function only.
o
To recall the drift or jitter values, use the
getDrift()
,
getJitterMax()
, and
getJitterMin()
functions.
